meaning.evidence: Every ingredient, quantity, temperature, time and storage note survives. Additions hang off the original: "(call it 220°C)" converts the given temperature, "or it'll turn out tough as old boots" explains the overmixing warning, "(good luck with that)" reacts to leftovers.

sense.evidence: Terms mostly fit: "knock up", "bung it in the oven", "whack it in", "Keep your mitts off it", "tea towel". "(supper, if you're posh about it)" misreads the original's "dinner (supper)" gloss; in Australia supper is a late snack, not a posh word for the evening meal.

authenticity.evidence: Sounds like an Aussie cook talking: "Crank the oven up", "give the pan or tin a good spray", "dish it up", "gettin' stuck in", "don't knock it till you've tried it".

register.evidence: A full level-4 kitchen yarn that still works as a recipe, with swearing at dad level: "some buggers".

tone.evidence: The friendly how-to tone survives and the steps stay clear, but a couple of asides tip into mild mockery of the dish: "Sounds a bit weird, I reckon".

flow.evidence: Reads naturally aloud: "Tip the batter into the pan and whack it in the oven."

variety.evidence: Wide range with no tic: "knock up", "feed", "brekkie", "bung", "whack", "tough as old boots", "mitts", "chuck".

essence.evidence: Still clearly the Wikibooks Southern Cornbread recipe, with its structure (intro, ingredients, equipment, procedure, notes) intact.

problems.why: Turns the original's regional gloss into a class joke; Australians would not hear "supper" as the posh word for the evening meal.

A.summary: A lively, natural level-4 recipe yarn that keeps every detail, adds a handy Celsius conversion and only harmless colour. One gloss is slightly mistranslated.

register.evidence: Almost entirely untranslated; a few insertions ("Now,", "Well,", "some buggers") are all that changes in a level-4 brief.

tone.evidence: The neutral recipe tone mostly survives because the text is untouched; "some buggers" adds an odd sneer.

flow.evidence: Broken joins: "Well, Pour the batter into the skillet", "lunch or tea (tea)", "Now, beat egg in the bowl."

variety.evidence: A couple of fillers ("Now," twice, "Well,") and one swear word; nothing to vary.

B.summary: The original with a few fillers and one swear word inserted, plus a garbled gloss. Far below the level-4 brief.

meaning.evidence: All quantities, steps and notes survive accurately: "Let it cool for 5 minutes in the pan before you serve it up", "kept in the fridge for a few days".

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "self-raising", "full-cream milk", "frypan", "baking tin", "lunch or dinner (tea, if you like)", "give it a spray of non-stick".

authenticity.evidence: Natural Australian kitchen talk: "Crank the oven up", "bung it in", "getting stuck into it", "don't overmix the bugger". "a doddle" is a Britishism.

register.evidence: Clearly Aussie and dad-level, but a notch lighter than level 4: headings and some lines stay close to the source ("Notes, tips, and variations", "Medium or large mixing bowl").

tone.evidence: Keeps the friendly, practical recipe voice without mocking the dish.

flow.evidence: Smooth throughout: "Stir in the cornmeal and mix till it's just wet through. The batter'll be a bit lumpy."

variety.evidence: Good range ("doddle", "dished up", "knock together", "brekkie", "bung", "whack"), though "frypan" recurs in nearly every step.

essence.evidence: Plainly the same recipe, in the same structure.

problems.why: "doddle" is British more than Australian; "dead easy" or "a cinch" would sound more local.
